text: Read beside the two laws Plato sets down for speech about the gods (Republic 379a–383c), Genesis 6 becomes a hard chapter. Yahweh "was grieved at his heart" and resolves to destroy every living thing (Genesis 6:6–7), so by Plato's standards he is both moved and a cause of harm. Plato framed his laws against gods who do evil out of caprice, the gods of Homer and Hesiod. The flood has a reason: "the earth was filled with violence" (Genesis 6:11). That reason narrows the conflict with Plato's laws but does not remove it. Socrates allows a god to punish if the poet can show the punishment just and the one punished made better by it (380a–b), and no one is made better by a flood. Grief Plato will not allow at all, because to be grieved is to be changed (381b–c). For Plato a good god cannot be affected by what is below him. For Genesis a good God is affected by what his creatures have become, and his grief shows how seriously he takes their corruption. Noah and Socrates also arrive at theology at different points in their building. Noah builds under God's judgment from the beginning. He works to dimensions handed down to him (Genesis 6:14–16) by a God who has looked at the world and been wounded by it. Socrates derives his city from human need (369b–c) and reaches theology only when the guardians must be educated (376c–e). Both texts read inner disorder on a larger scale. Genesis moves from "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart" (6:5) to an earth filled with violence, and Socrates looks for justice written larger in a city (368d–e). When the readings break off, both constructions are unfinished: the ark is waiting for its passengers, and the city is waiting for its rulers.
